u:libyan air force|map:wheelus.headline: The Libyan Air Force was built up with U.S. help from Wheelus, and after the U.S. left it used the base, renamed Okba Ben Nafi.
u:libyan air force|map:wheelus.explanation: Three U.S. government documents tie the Libyan Air Force to Wheelus at different stages. A 1969 meeting treated U.S. influence over the air force as something to use in talks about Wheelus's future. A later Kissinger memo says U.S. airmen at Wheelus helped the Libyans start their air force, and that this support would end when the U.S. left in June (1970). The link shows how a U.S. base became a Libyan military one after the 1969 revolution.

The U.S. provided training and second-level maintenance to the Libyan Air Force, and F-5 jets were to be delivered (DOC 2). The memo says ten F-5s had been delivered and eight more were scheduled.
The 1971 estimate says Okba Ben Nafi (formerly Wheelus) Air Base is used by the Libyan Air Force, assisted by Greek and Pakistani training missions.
not_established: The sources do not say how many Libyan Air Force units were based there, or which aircraft.

u:map:tajura-camp|ounianga kebir old air.explanation: Two copies of the same 1983 imagery analysis note cover both places under the title "Libya-Chad Conflict". At Tajura, near Tripoli, it reports a high level of heavy-lift transporter activity and tanks being loaded. At Ounianga Kebir in Chad, it reports more defensive measures. The title and layout suggest the analysts saw the two as parts of one Libyan effort. The passages we have do not say that the equipment from Tajura went to Ounianga Kebir. That is an inference. It matters because it shows Tajura as a staging point for Libya's military operations abroad.
established: The note is dated 16 August 1983 and is titled for Tajura Barracks and Vehicle Storage Area, Libya, and Ounianga Kebir Old Airfield, Chad.
It reports a high level of heavy-lift transporter activity at Tajura, with at least five probable tanks loaded and at least 34 empty transporters remaining.
It reports an increase in defensive measures at Ounianga Kebir old airfield.
Both documents are copies of the same note, so they are not two independent sources.
not_established: The visible text does not say that vehicles loaded at Tajura were taken to Ounianga Kebir.
The passages are cut off, and part of the original was withheld, so the full reasoning is missing.
The AI summaries mention guns and armour at Ounianga Kebir, but the text we have does not show that detail.
